messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Policy Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi had always taken pride in his sharp mind and quick wit. As a policy analyst for over three decades, he was used to digging through complex data and crafting sound recommendations. But all of that changed two years ago when he received the devastating diagnosis: stage IV prostate cancer. The words still echoed in his mind like a death sentence. The treatment that followed was grueling – rounds of chemotherapy, radiation, and endless doctor's appointments. Kofi tried to stay focused on his work, but it became increasingly difficult to concentrate. His mind would wander back to the hospital room where he received the diagnosis, reliving the moment when his whole world came crashing down. Even now, as he sat in his living room, trying to read a report or watch TV, he found himself drifting away, his thoughts hijacked by the memory of that fateful day. Sometimes, Kofi would recall the details of his treatment with an eerie detachment – feeling like he was observing someone else's life. Other times, the memories came flooding back in vivid, terrifying detail. He'd be sitting at home when suddenly he was back in the hospital bed, surrounded by beeping machines and antiseptic smells, his body wracked with pain. The memory felt so real, so present, that Kofi would have to stop whatever he was doing, overcome by a wave of emotion. Kofi's body had become his greatest enemy. Even now, long after the treatment had ended, it still reacted as if danger lurked around every corner. His muscles remained tense and coiled, ready to spring into action at the slightest provocation. He'd catch himself holding his breath or flinching at a sudden noise – an innocuous sound that, in another life, would have passed unnoticed. At home, Kofi felt like he was walking on eggshells, waiting for the other shoe to drop. He couldn't shake the feeling that something was off, even when everything seemed fine. He'd wake up in the middle of the night, his heart racing, with no clear reason why. His body had betrayed him once; Kofi wasn't sure he could ever trust it again. The numbness he felt – not just about his emotions but also about life itself – terrified Kofi. Would he ever be able to feel normal emotions again? Or would this flatline continue indefinitely, a constant reminder of the fragility of his own mortality? He longed for the days when laughter came easily and tears didn't seem like an existential threat. Kofi's work began to suffer as well. Colleagues noticed a change in him – a once-sharp mind now dulled by distraction and anxiety. Projects piled up, deadlines loomed, and Kofi found himself unable to concentrate on even the simplest tasks. His confidence waned; his sense of self-worth dwindled. It was only when he realized that his grandchildren were starting to notice the change in him – their once-vibrant grandfather now a shadow of his former self – that Kofi finally sought help. He knew he couldn't keep living like this, trapped in a world where memories haunted him and his body felt like a minefield waiting to be triggered. As he sat in his therapist's office for the first time, Kofi felt a glimmer of hope – maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this labyrinth. But what scared him most was the thought that it might already be too late, that the damage had been done and all he could do now was try to pick up the pieces of a life forever shattered by illness and fear.
